oneSentence: Information organised into predefined fields, often in rows and columns, so software can process it predictably.
plainExplanation:
Structured data is information arranged in a fixed pattern. Usually that means rows and columns, like a spreadsheet or database table. Each row describes one item, and each column holds one type of value, such as date, country, budget or status.

What goes in? Clear fields and consistent formats. For example, a programme table might have one row per project and columns for project code, start date, region and spending. If dates use the same format and regions use the same names, the data is easier for software to work with.

What happens next? Software can search, sort, filter, join and count the data. "Join" means linking two tables using a shared field, such as project code. Because the structure is regular, a model or reporting tool can quickly answer questions like "Which projects in East Africa started in 2024?" or "What is the average spend by region?"

What comes out? Summaries, charts, alerts, recommendations and model inputs. Structured data is often easier to check and govern than free text, but it can still contain errors, missing values or outdated categories. It is different from unstructured data, such as long documents, images or audio, which do not come in neat columns by default.

everydayAnalogy.title: A well-organised library card cabinet
everydayAnalogy.story: In a library, staff keep a cabinet of index cards for each document in the knowledge base. Every card has the same boxes: title, language, topic, year and shelf code. Because the boxes are always in the same place, a librarian can quickly pull all French-language health reports from 2023. If some cards use different topic names or leave the year blank, the search becomes less reliable.

mapping.aiElement: the same columns or fields for each record

mapping.analogyElement: pulling cards by topic, language and year

everydayAnalogy.limitation: Real structured data is not limited to paper-like cards. It can live in databases, update automatically and be linked across many tables. Also, some useful data is only partly regular, so the neat-card image can hide the fact that many real systems mix structured, semi-structured and unstructured information.

visual.title: From records to usable analysis
visual.learningObjective: Show how consistent rows and columns let software turn records into filters, counts and model-ready inputs.
visual.description: A left-to-right flow with four panels. Read from raw records, to named columns, to software operations, to outputs. Each panel shows the same small dataset becoming easier to analyse because fields stay consistent across rows.

steps.label: Records collected
steps.explanation: Start with several items to track, such as documents or projects. Each item becomes one row.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a small table with 4 rows and faint placeholders, labelled 'one row = one item'.

steps.label: Fields standardised
steps.explanation: Each column has one meaning, such as title, country, date or budget. Formats are made consistent.
steps.visualInstruction: Show column headers in bold: title, country, year, topic. Add a small note: 'same field meaning in every row'.

steps.label: Software operates on the table
steps.explanation: Because the layout is regular, software can sort, filter, count and combine tables using shared fields.
steps.visualInstruction: Add icons or simple labels above the table: sort, filter, count, join. Draw arrows from the table to these labels.

steps.label: Useful outputs
steps.explanation: The same data can feed dashboards, reports, alerts or AI systems that expect clearly defined inputs.
steps.visualInstruction: Show four output boxes: chart, summary table, recommendation list, model input. Connect them from the operations stage.

visual.interaction: Hovering or tapping each stage highlights the relevant part of the table and shows one example question, such as 'count projects by region' or 'find documents in Arabic from 2022'.
visual.accessibilityDescription: The diagram explains why regular structure matters. First, several items are collected, with one row representing one item. Next, the rows are organised into columns with fixed meanings such as title, country, year and topic. Then software can perform operations on those columns, including sorting, filtering, counting and joining with another table using a shared field. Finally, these operations produce outputs such as charts, summary tables, recommendation lists or model-ready inputs. The key idea is that consistent fields make reliable processing possible.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static four-panel flow shows the same dataset moving from collected records, to standardised columns, to software operations, to outputs, without animation. Highlight colours and labels replace motion.

workedExample.scenario: A small knowledge base team wants to recommend documents about drought response.
workedExample.input: A table with columns: document_id, title, language, topic, region, year. Example rows include D014 | Seasonal drought outlook | English | climate | East Africa | 2024 and D022 | Water access assessment | French | water | Sahel | 2023.
process: The team stores each document as one row and uses the same column names for all records.
A user asks for recent French documents on water issues in the Sahel.
The system filters rows where language = French, topic = water and region = Sahel.
It sorts the remaining rows by year, newest first, and returns the top matches.
workedExample.result: The output is a short, relevant list, such as D022 first, followed by other rows that match the same fields. This works well because the metadata is structured and consistent.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: A programme team reviews monitoring data from several country offices in a shared reporting system. Each row represents one project activity, with columns for location, reporting period, output code, planned value and actual value.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: Because the fields are standardised, staff can compare progress across offices, spot missing reports and produce dashboards more reliably than if updates only arrived as narrative emails.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Do not place personal, confidential or protection-sensitive records into an unapproved public AI service. Use approved systems, apply access controls and check that field definitions mean the same thing across offices before comparing results.

whyItMatters: Structured data affects what questions software can answer quickly and safely. If data is well organised, teams can compare like with like, automate routine reporting and feed tools with cleaner inputs. If it is badly structured, results can be misleading even when the chart or model looks polished. For non-specialists, this matters in procurement, oversight and daily operations: before trusting an output, ask whether the underlying fields are consistent, complete and current. Good structure does not guarantee truth, but poor structure often guarantees extra work and higher risk.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If information is in a spreadsheet, it is automatically high quality structured data.
commonMisconceptions.correction: A spreadsheet can still contain merged cells, mixed date formats, blank values, duplicate rows or columns that change meaning. The container is not the same as the quality of the structure.
Structured data can include text categories too, such as country names, language codes or status labels. What makes it structured is the consistent field layout, not whether the values are numeric.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Structured data is always better than unstructured data.
commonMisconceptions.correction: It is easier for many systems to process, but it can leave out nuance found in documents, images or audio. Many real tasks need both: structured fields for consistency and unstructured material for context.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: It is information arranged the same way every time, usually in rows and columns, so software can handle it predictably.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: Structured data uses a predefined schema, meaning an agreed layout of fields, data types and relationships. In practice, this often appears as relational database tables or well-formed spreadsheet columns where each row is a record and each column represents one attribute with a consistent meaning. Because the schema is stable, systems can validate values, index fields for fast search, aggregate across records, and join tables through keys such as an ID code. This differs from unstructured data, where the useful information is embedded in free text, images or audio rather than placed into fixed fields from the start.

keyTakeaway: The more consistently information fits into named fields, the easier it is for software to analyse it reliably.

quickCheck.question: Which example best fits structured data?
options: A folder of scanned letters with no labels beyond file names
A table where each row is a project and columns include country, start date, budget and status
A video recording of a meeting stored as one media file
A long narrative report pasted into one spreadsheet cell per document
quickCheck.explanation: Structured data uses consistent fields for each record. The project table has a regular layout that software can sort, filter and analyse. The other examples may contain useful information, but not in a fixed column-based structure.

issues.problem: This defines structured data too narrowly as rows and columns. Tabular data is a common form, but structured data is defined by a predefined schema and can use other arrangements.
issues.fix: Information organised into predefined fields, often in rows and columns, so software can process it predictably.

issues.problem: The example does not define what counts as "recent", so it cannot establish that D022 from 2023 meets the request. It also provides only one matching row, so the claimed ordering cannot be checked. There is no arithmetic in this example to compute.
issues.fix: D022 passes the three stated category filters, while D014 does not. A year rule is still needed to decide whether D022 is recent.

issues.problem: The visual implies that consistent structure alone makes data model-ready. A regular schema helps, but the data may still require validation, cleaning or transformation, as the page itself notes elsewhere.
issues.fix: Replace "model-ready inputs" with "clearly defined model inputs" and replace "model-ready inputs" in the accessibility description with "model inputs with clearly defined fields".

issues.problem: The fourth option is also defensible. A table with one row per document and one consistent text field has structured records containing unstructured text. The explanation incorrectly claims that this option has no fixed column-based structure. Options 0 and 2 are unstructured files, while option 1 is clearly structured.
issues.fix: A spreadsheet where merged cells and changing columns arrange each report differently
